divergent/dotted-name-context-precedence: the package follows the SPECIFICATION and mustache.js does not. `{{#a}}{{b.c}}{{/a}}` over {"a":{"b":{}},"b":{"c":"ERROR"}} must render nothing: the specification's `Dotted Names - Context Precedence` case says each part of a dotted name resolves only against its parent, so the enclosing `b` is not a fallback for the `b` inside `a`. mustache.js resumes the search at the outer frame and renders `ERROR` -- it is the one required-module case the reference implementation fails, which `diff.mjs spec` reports on every run.
divergent/interpolate-collection.json: interpolating an array or an object is undefined: the specification never does it, so each implementation falls back to its host language. mustache.js reaches JavaScript's String(), which is `[object Object]` for an object and a comma-join for an array. The package writes compact JSON instead -- deterministic, identical on every platform, and legible.
whitespace is ASCII whitespace here. The tag sits on a line whose only other character is a NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0). JavaScript's `\s` counts that as whitespace, so mustache.js finds the line standalone and removes it; the package treats it as content, so the line survives. Every character Mustache gives meaning to is ASCII, and a byte-level scan is what makes the tokenizer exact.
divergent/three-delimiters.json: `{{=a b c=}}` names three delimiters. mustache.js splits on whitespace with a limit of 2 and silently uses the first two, so the trailing `c` disappears and `aXb` interpolates. The package refuses the tag with errorCode::ErrInvalidFormat: a set-delimiters tag that does not name exactly two delimiters is a typo, and guessing which two were meant changes what every following tag in the template means.
